text: The cow's stomach is unusual, with four compartments, each made of different tissue adapted to its function. The rumen sits on the left side of the body and has a volume of about 160 liters. The reticulum has a volume of about 9.5 liters; the spleen sits against the reticulum (and partly against the rumen). The omasum has a volume of about 15 liters. The abomasum is called the 'true stomach', functioning the same way as the pig's single stomach, and holds about 20 liters. After the four stomachs, the digestive tract continues with the small intestine (about 40 m long, running from the abomasum to the large intestine) and the large intestine (about 10 m long, continuing to the rectum). Glands connected to the digestive tract include the liver (4–10 kg, not clearly divided into lobes; its duct joins the gall bladder duct and opens into the small intestine) and the pancreas.
